stem: A client with type 2 diabetes who takes empagliflozin presents with nausea, vomiting, abdominal discomfort, and fatigue. The blood glucose is 210 mg/dL. Which complication must still be considered?

options.A: Diabetic ketoacidosis, because SGLT2-associated ketoacidosis can occur even when the presenting glucose is below 250 mg/dL.
options.B: Hyperosmolar hyperglycemic state, established solely by the glucose value of 210 mg/dL without additional testing.
options.C: Hypoglycemia, because SGLT2-related ketoacidosis requires glucose above 300 mg/dL.
options.D: Medication intolerance only; ketones and acid-base status do not need evaluation at this glucose level.

rationale: The current JARDIANCE (empagliflozin) label warns that diabetic ketoacidosis and other ketoacidosis can occur with SGLT2 inhibitors and that blood glucose at presentation may be below the levels typically expected for DKA, including below 250 mg/dL. Nausea, vomiting, abdominal pain, malaise, dehydration, and shortness of breath are compatible symptoms. The label directs clinicians to assess for ketoacidosis regardless of presenting blood glucose and to promptly evaluate if it is suspected. Therefore A is correct. B cannot be established from glucose 210 mg/dL, C falsely requires marked hyperglycemia for SGLT2-associated DKA, and D would inappropriately dismiss a potentially life-threatening adverse effect.
educational_objective: Recognize that SGLT2-associated DKA can present with only modest hyperglycemia and evaluate compatible symptoms for ketones and metabolic acidosis regardless of the presenting glucose level.
source_organization: DailyMed / U.S. Food and Drug Administration labeling
source_version_date: Updated February 17, 2026; prescribing information revised January 2026
source_locator: Warnings and Precautions §5.1: signs/symptoms include nausea, vomiting, abdominal pain, malaise, dyspnea; blood glucose may be below typical DKA levels (e.g., <250 mg/dL); assess for ketoacidosis regardless of presenting glucose; discontinue and promptly evaluate/treat if suspected.
source_claim_supported: Empagliflozin-associated DKA/ketoacidosis can occur with glucose below 250 mg/dL, so compatible symptoms warrant evaluation regardless of the presenting glucose level.
blueprint_source_organization: National Council of State Boards of Nursing (NCSBN)
blueprint_locator: Pharmacological and Parenteral Therapies: recognize serious medication adverse effects, monitor therapy, interpret relevant laboratory findings, and intervene for medication-related complications.
blueprint_topic: Pharmacological and Parenteral Therapies — SGLT2 inhibitor ketoacidosis recognition

source_original.stem: A client taking an SGLT2 inhibitor presents with nausea, vomiting, abdominal discomfort, and fatigue. The blood glucose is 210 mg/dL. Which complication must still be considered?

options.A: Diabetic ketoacidosis should still be evaluated because SGLT2-associated ketoacidosis may occur with glucose below 250 mg/dL.
options.B: Hyperosmolar hyperglycemic state is established by the glucose value of 210 mg/dL without additional testing.
options.C: Hypoglycemia is the likely metabolic emergency because SGLT2-related ketoacidosis requires glucose above 300 mg/dL.
options.D: The symptoms can be attributed to medication intolerance without checking ketones or acid-base status at this glucose level.

source_original.rationale: FDA warns that ketoacidosis with SGLT2 inhibitors may occur with blood glucose below 250 mg/dL. Compatible symptoms should prompt assessment for ketones and metabolic acidosis rather than dismissing DKA because glucose is only modestly elevated.
source_original.source_detail: Warnings and Precautions §5.1 — Ketoacidosis; evaluate compatible symptoms regardless of presenting blood glucose. Revised 01/2026; live DailyMed label currentness rechecked 2026-08-15. NCSBN first-check: Client Needs — Physiological Integrity — Pharmacological and Parenteral Therapies: medication administration, adverse effects/interactions, monitoring, reconciliation and teaching. 2026 NCLEX-RN Test Plan; effective 2026-04-01 through 2029-03-31; currentness rechecked 2026-08-15.

correction_summary: Retained the SGLT2-ketoacidosis construct and key A, but specified type 2 diabetes so the DKA label is clinically unambiguous, preserved the FDA-supported <250 mg/dL point, and reduced difficulty from hard to medium because the final item tests a direct serious-adverse-effect recognition rule.

audit_findings.source_authority: Current DailyMed/FDA empagliflozin label; official NCSBN 2026 blueprint
audit_findings.claim_audit: Final item accurately reflects the labeled symptom pattern and the instruction to assess for ketoacidosis regardless of presenting glucose. It does not diagnose DKA from symptoms alone; it asks which complication must still be considered/evaluated.

distractor_audit.B: Incorrect because HHS is not established by glucose 210 mg/dL and requires a different hyperglycemic/hyperosmolar pattern.
distractor_audit.C: Incorrect because SGLT2-associated DKA can occur below 250 mg/dL.
distractor_audit.D: Incorrect because compatible symptoms require ketoacidosis evaluation rather than dismissal as intolerance.

audit_findings.ambiguity_second_answer: Only A matches the stated SGLT2 exposure, compatible symptoms, and modest glucose without asserting a diagnosis from incomplete data.
audit_findings.cueing: All alternatives are metabolic/medication interpretations of the same presentation; the correct response is based on the specific FDA warning rather than an unrelated cue.
audit_findings.blueprint: Pharmacological and Parenteral Therapies — serious adverse-effect recognition and monitoring.
audit_findings.independent_second_pass: Rechecked the January 2026 prescribing information/February 2026 DailyMed update, §5.1 symptom and glucose language, all options, rationale, objective, difficulty, ambiguity, cueing, and NCSBN mapping. A remained uniquely correct.
